touches.text: An internal device is its own process. An external device depends on what it wraps (5.8.3.7).
A device may own other processes besides its own; they are inside its boundary. Eg Cairn owns the bus process and the ground loop.
A device's code lives in cairn/devices/<device>/; its data in ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/.
The instance is a number; a singleton is 0. A bare name addresses instance 0 (`cc` means `cc 0`); the number is written only when it isn't 0.
Nothing in a device's code differs by instance.
A device owns its state: only the device writes under its own ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ tree.

Machine: tools plus the glue that holds them together. Has an owner. Anything that calls a machine or device, or owns state it must gate, is a machine. Lives inside its device (cairn/devices/<device>/machines/<machine>/), or in cairn/machines/ when several devices hold one (16).
Device: its own process, in the rack, on the bus (2).

A retirement checks its callers in the same act as the deletion: nothing imports the module being deleted, and nothing runs the command or path being deleted. A file that only names it (a fixture, a record, a charter) is not a caller. Nothing checks afterwards. Why? Naming is history; only a caller breaks, and a caller that comes later breaks loudly on its own. A standing proof that a thing stays gone is history kept as code.

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.

Repo-root bin/ holds only the launcher itself, the one thing on PATH. Every shortcut lives in the bin/ of the device or machine it belongs to; its bin/ plus its bus verbs is what help lists at that level.

An instance is declared by its folder existing in class-space: cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ (one address in two roots). Declared = the folders (read by the rack tool, 17.20); running = which of those are in the rack.

Every device has a shim. Each shim is its own process, one per instance, and connects to the bus as a client. WHY: in the bus process, updating one shim meant bringing the whole bus down, and one shim's stall was everyone's. Separate, a shim restarts itself when its own files change, like the ground loop, and the bus stays up.
Writes its runtime data, if any, to ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/.
INTENTION:
sudo_relay (machine): Recovery's way to root on Linux, needed for installs and upgrades.
A command goes in, runs as root, and a permanent audit record comes out: the command line, return code, stdout, stderr, plus an id and date. The audit folder keeps a rolling one month.
A machine, not a tool: it keeps the audit records (state it must gate), and runs as its own root process inside Recovery's boundary (2.3.2.1).
Other platforms get their own way to root (eg on Windows, Rescue and the installer run from an elevated PowerShell, 6.5.3.3).

Any device may ask Recovery to run something as root. The operator answers each ask: decline, accept now, accept always, accept with a new rule, or (for a chat-enabled device) chat about it. Cairn owns it.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.
Instance: every device has at least one; a singleton is instance 0.

conflicts.why: Outline explicitly states: 'Repo-root bin/ holds only the launcher itself' and 'Every shortcut lives in the bin/ of the device or machine it belongs to.' After sudo_relay becomes a machine inside Recovery, its shortcut must move from repo-root bin/cmd/ to Recovery's bin/, not remain at repo-root.
